God appears directly to this non-Israelite prophet and refuses ("for they are blessed", tying back to Genesis 12:3), Balaam reports the refusal honestly, but a second, more honorable delegation gets a conditional yes (go, but speak only what I tell you). The chapter's dramatic core: the angel of the LORD blocks the road three times with a drawn sword, visible only to Balaam's donkey, who is beaten three times for saving her rider's life without his knowledge; God opens the donkey's mouth (2 Peter 2:16 callback) and then Balaam's own eyes, and the angel reveals Balaam would have been killed had the donkey not turned away. Closes with Balak meeting Balaam at the border, repeating his bribe, and taking him up into the high places of Baal to view only part of Israel's camp, setting up the oracles in chapters 23-24. entries.notes: Scheduled hourly Bible Note Writer Agent run. The first two of Balaam's three oracles: Balak builds seven altars with seven oxen and seven rams (repeated at each of three sites), and Balaam delivers a poetic oracle declaring Israel cannot be cursed because God already blessed them ("how shall I curse, whom God hath not cursed"), echoing the dust-of-the-earth promise to Abraham (Genesis 13:16) and Israel's set-apart identity as a nation. Balak, shocked at the blessing instead of a curse, drags Balaam to a second site, the field of Zophim atop Pisgah (the same mountain Moses later views the promised land from in Deuteronomy 34:1), for a second oracle centered on God's unchanging character ("God is not a man, that he should lie"), His irreversible commitment to bless, and vivid lion/conquest imagery, including the now-famous phrase "what hath God wrought" (later the first telegraph message, 1844). Closes with Balak, now only hoping for silence rather than a curse, taking Balaam to a third site at Peor, linked to Baal-peor and the coming crisis in Numbers 25. entries.notes: Scheduled hourly Bible Note Writer Agent run. Balaam's third oracle, given this time without seeking any omens at all -- the Spirit of God comes on him directly as he simply looks at Israel's ordered tribal camp, and he pours out an oracle of thriving abundance (lign aloes, cedar trees, overflowing water imagery) that closes by repeating God's original covenant promise to Abraham almost word for word ("blessed is he that blesseth thee," Genesis 12:3). Balak's fury boils over ("smote his hands together") and he dismisses Balaam, who restates one final time that he never had power to go beyond the LORD's command, matching his own words from Numbers 22:18. Before leaving, Balaam delivers a fourth, unrequested oracle reaching into "the latter days" -- the messianic "Star out of Jacob" and "Sceptre out of Israel" prophecy (paired with Judah's sceptre blessing in Genesis 49:10, later read as pointing toward Matthew 2's star), plus near-term predictions against Moab and Edom historically fulfilled by David in 2 Samuel 8. Closes with short oracles against Amalek, the Kenites, and a widening view to Asshur/Eber/Chittim (Cyprus/the Mediterranean coastlands), then both men simply going their separate ways -- Balaam reappearing later as an antagonist in Numbers 31:8. Israel's full appointed-offerings calendar: the daily continual offering (two lambs, morning and evening, with grain and wine, first ordained at Sinai in Exodus 29:38-42), the doubled Sabbath offering, the monthly New Moon offering (introducing the standard 'two bullocks, one ram, seven lambs' big-occasion package plus the chapter's first sin offering), Passover and the seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread (holy convocations bookending the week, the same big-occasion package repeated daily), and the Feast of Firstfruits/Weeks (the future Pentecost, counted 49 days out per Leviticus 23:15-16). Density ~1.02 cards/verse (55 verses). entries.notes: Scheduled hourly run. Style redo backlog empty, normal forward progress, first dedicated file for this chapter. David stays home from the spring campaign season while Joab besieges Rabbah, sees Bathsheba bathing from the palace roof and sends for her despite the servant naming both her father Eliam (likely one of David's mighty men) and her husband Uriah the Hittite. She conceives, and the note that she was purified from her uncleanness rules out Uriah as the father since he is away at war. David recalls Uriah under cover of a war briefing and twice tries to send him home to his wife (a royal food gift, then getting him drunk), but Uriah sleeps at the palace door out of loyalty to his fellow soldiers and the ark in the field both times. David escalates to murder by proxy, sending Uriah back to Joab carrying his own death order; Joab places him where the city's strongest defenders are and coaches the messenger with the Abimelech/Jerubbesheth callback to Judges 9 in case David objects to the risky tactics. David instead brushes off the report with the proverb about the sword devouring one as well as another once he hears Uriah is dead. The chapter closes with Bathsheba's mourning, David's marriage to her that makes the affair look resolved, undercut by the final sentence naming God's own verdict for the first time in the chapter. Chunked into 9 sections (1, 2-3, 4-5, 6-9, 10-13, 14-17, 18-21, 22-25, 26-27).
